strengths: The paper introduces a simple and practically meaningful middle ground between target-free and full target-network methods: retaining frozen linear heads while sharing the feature extractor substantially reduces parameter storage.
The method is clearly specified, easy to implement, and naturally extends iterated Q-learning to a much more memory-efficient architecture.

The empirical study is reasonably broad within discrete value-based RL, covering online DQN and offline CQL, two network architectures, normalized and unnormalized variants, 10–15 Atari games, and five seeds per game.

Results consistently show substantial improvements over the corresponding target-free baselines. In several settings the method approaches or exceeds the full target-network baseline while using roughly half as many network parameters.

The use of per-game curves, IQM aggregation, stratified bootstrap confidence intervals, effective-rank measurements, and gradient-similarity diagnostics improves the credibility and interpretability of the findings.
weaknesses: The central systems claims are incompletely validated. The paper reports parameter counts rather than measured peak VRAM, and provides no wall-clock time or throughput results despite repeatedly claiming comparable training time and a smaller memory footprint. Optimizer state, activations, replay memory, and computation across multiple heads should be included in an end-to-end comparison.

The baseline set is limited. Most comparisons use a naive target-free version of DQN or CQL; the paper does not empirically compare against the stronger target-free or regularized methods discussed in related work. Consequently, the broad claim of improving target-free approaches is supported less strongly than the framing suggests.

Several design choices are insufficiently ablated. In particular, behavior actions are sampled from a uniformly selected head, the loss sums K temporal-difference objectives, and K is varied on the evaluation games. The gains could partly reflect altered exploration, auxiliary-loss regularization, or increased update signal rather than learning consecutive Bellman iterations specifically.

The selection of K appears based on the same benchmark results used for reporting, with different preferred values across architectures. There is no held-out selection protocol, robustness analysis, or practical rule for choosing K, creating a risk of benchmark-level tuning.
The evaluation is confined to Atari discrete control. No continuous-control, non-visual, or larger-scale task is included, so the generality and practical scaling motivation remain uncertain.

The explanatory analyses are correlational: greater gradient agreement with the target-based method and higher feature rank do not establish that either causes the performance improvement. Stability measures such as value magnitude, divergence frequency, or target drift would provide more direct evidence.

Reproducibility is not yet complete because the manuscript only promises that code will be released. Some reporting details are also missing, including explicit numerical result tables, measured computational cost, and a clearer account of how uncertainty for ratios normalized by the target-based AUC is computed.

The method is evaluated in several settings, including online and offline Atari, CNN and IMPALA architectures, with and without LayerNorm.
The experiments use five seeds, per-game learning curves, IQM aggregation, and stratified bootstrap confidence intervals, which are preferable to reporting only mean final performance.
The K=1 result usefully isolates the effect of retaining a frozen last layer, while the K sweeps provide some evidence about the benefit and limits of additional heads.
weaknesses: The central algorithm is an incremental combination of shared multi-head representations and previously proposed iterated Q-learning. The paper does not establish sufficiently strong conceptual or technical novelty beyond this combination for a top-tier venue.

The claim that the heads represent consecutive Bellman iterations is not rigorously justified: although the first head is frozen, its shared feature extractor is updated by all losses, so every represented Q-function changes simultaneously. No convergence or stability analysis explains the consequences of this coupling.

The evaluation lacks important controls. In particular, there is no parameter-matched single-network multi-head baseline, auxiliary-head baseline without the Bellman chain, or capacity-matched target-based baseline. Consequently, the gains cannot be cleanly attributed to iterated Bellman learning rather than multi-task representation learning or additional output heads.

K is swept extensively and the best values differ across architectures, but no validation or selection protocol is specified. Reporting the favorable configuration on the same games used for evaluation creates a substantial model-selection concern.

The motivating efficiency claims are inadequately validated. Parameter counts are not equivalent to actual peak VRAM, and the paper reports no measured peak memory, wall-clock throughput, or training time despite claiming comparable training time and emphasizing memory savings. Activations, optimizer state, replay storage, and computation from multiple losses are omitted from the comparison.

The empirical scope remains narrow: all results use discrete-action Atari, with only 10–15 selected games rather than the standard broader suite. The offline experiment uses one restricted dataset construction, and there are no modern strong value-based baselines or continuous-control results.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Code is only promised for future release, and important implementation details—such as the precise CQL objective and coefficient, LayerNorm placement, evaluation protocol, and configuration-selection procedure—are missing or underspecified.

The mechanistic evidence is correlational. Gradient similarity and effective rank do not demonstrate improved stability or explain causality, and several relevant confidence intervals overlap. Overall, the experiments show improvement over the target-free baseline but do not support the broader explanatory and efficiency claims strongly enough for acceptance.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, clear, and practically relevant middle ground between target-free and conventional target-network Q-learning: retaining only frozen linear heads while sharing the feature extractor substantially reduces parameter storage.
Combining shared features with iterated Q-learning is a meaningful contribution. The resulting iS-QN formulation is easy to implement and applies to both DQN and CQL.

The empirical results are consistently favorable: iS-DQN narrows or closes the target-free performance gap across CNN, CNN plus LayerNorm, and IMPALA architectures, while iS-CQL reduces the reported offline gap from 26% to 6%.
The evaluation covers online and offline learning, multiple architectures, 10–15 Atari games, five seeds per game, per-game curves, IQM aggregation, and stratified bootstrap confidence intervals.

Ablations over the number of heads show when additional Bellman iterations help and where performance saturates or declines. The K=1 experiments also isolate the benefit of retaining only the last target layer.

The gradient-similarity, effective-rank, and ensemble-shared-feature analyses provide useful—albeit correlational—evidence about why shared target heads may improve optimization and representation quality.
The method achieves its primary empirical goal while using close to the target-free model's parameter count, making it potentially useful when network-parameter storage is a bottleneck.
weaknesses: The central systems claim is evaluated using parameter count rather than actual peak VRAM, wall-clock time, throughput, or FLOPs. Target networks do not require gradient or optimizer-state storage, whereas multiple simultaneous losses may increase activation and compute costs; therefore, the claimed memory and training-time advantages are not fully established.

The method's target is not genuinely frozen because the shared feature extractor changes every gradient step; only the linear head is frozen. The paper would benefit from a more precise stability analysis or theoretical characterization of this moving target.

The mechanistic evidence is correlational. Greater gradient alignment with TB-DQN and higher effective rank do not demonstrate that either property causes the performance improvement, and the gradient analysis covers only an early portion of training.

The experimental scope is narrower than standard comprehensive Atari evaluation: results use selected subsets of 10 or 15 games rather than the full suite, and the offline study is limited to one benchmark family and dataset regime. Continuous-control generalization is left unexplored.

The choice of K is effectively tuned across several values on the reported benchmark, but no validation protocol or robust default-selection rule is given. Performance also degrades at large K in some settings, which limits the claim that more Bellman iterations generally improve performance.

Comparisons focus primarily on the target-based and target-free versions of the authors' implementation. Broader comparisons with strong contemporary memory-efficient or target-free approaches would better establish the method's relative significance.

The paper states that the code will be released rather than providing an available artifact, and some method-specific details—especially complete CQL loss construction and direct resource measurements—are insufficient for fully confident reproduction.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple, clearly motivated middle ground between target-free and full target-network methods: retain frozen linear heads while sharing the feature extractor, then use multiple heads to approximate successive Bellman updates.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, spanning online Atari, offline Atari, continuous control on DMC Hard, and language-based offline RL with GPT-2/Wordle. Results consistently improve over the corresponding target-free baselines and often approach or exceed full target-network performance.
The study uses reasonably strong architectures and algorithms, including IMPALA, CQL, SimbaV2/SAC, and ILQL, rather than demonstrating the idea only on a small or outdated benchmark.

Evaluation methodology is generally careful: multiple seeds, aggregate results across tasks, IQM statistics, stratified bootstrap confidence intervals, per-task learning curves, and parameter and runtime comparisons are provided.
The analysis of gradient alignment, target churn, feature rank, and dormant neurons offers useful empirical evidence about why partially frozen heads may stabilize learning.

The method provides substantial parameter savings in settings where the critic or language model dominates model storage, while introducing only small heads and little apparent runtime overhead. Hyperparameters and implementation details are also documented extensively.
weaknesses: The central resource-efficiency claim is supported mainly by parameter counts, not measured peak training VRAM or total memory. Activations, optimizer states, gradients, replay buffers, and framework overhead can dominate memory, so the practical savings—especially for edge-device motivation—remain insufficiently established.

Several comparisons are not fully controlled. For example, the DMC target-based SAC baseline omits BatchNorm while target-free and iS-SAC use it; behavior policies also differ through random head selection or averaging across heads. These choices make it difficult to isolate the contribution of shared frozen heads and iterated Bellman targets.

Increasing K simultaneously adds auxiliary losses, changes behavior/exploration, and enriches representation learning. The paper lacks decisive controls such as multiple heads predicting the same target, parameter-matched auxiliary heads, a shared-head ensemble in all settings, and direct comparisons against the original full iterated Q-network under matched memory or compute.

The sum of K losses changes the optimization problem as K varies. Dismissing learning-rate or loss-normalization controls because Adam normalizes gradients is not sufficient: Adam does not eliminate changes in gradient scale, variance, or relative weighting. The continuous-control experiment additionally introduces an empirically chosen 0.25 discount over losses.

There is no convergence or stability analysis for the proposed shared-feature construction. Because the supposedly frozen target heads consume features that change after every update, standard fixed-target intuition does not directly apply; the target-churn measurements are informative but do not establish technical guarantees.

The best K varies considerably by architecture and domain, and values up to 49 are evaluated without a principled selection rule. Since performance claims often report the favorable K, the cost and robustness of tuning this new hyperparameter are understated.

Some headline gains are modest or statistically ambiguous: target-free ILQL is not significantly worse than target-based ILQL, and iS-SAC K=9 offers little improvement over K=1. Wordle is also only a single task with five seeds, so the language-model scaling conclusion is preliminary.

The reported normalized AUC procedure appears to divide confidence intervals by a point estimate of the target-based IQM rather than jointly bootstrapping the ratio; if so, uncertainty in the denominator and paired experimental structure are not fully represented. End-of-training performance is also secondary despite being relevant to several claims.

The empirical study is unusually broad, covering online Atari, offline Atari, continuous control, and offline language RL, with several architectures and base algorithms.

The paper reports robust aggregate statistics, confidence intervals, per-task learning curves, runtime/FLOP measurements, and diagnostic analyses of target churn, gradient similarity, and representation rank.
Across the evaluated settings, the method consistently improves over the corresponding target-free baseline, and the K=1 results suggest that partial target sharing alone can be beneficial.

The manuscript is generally clear and provides pseudocode, hyperparameter tables, and implementation details. weaknesses: The central resource-efficiency claim is not adequately validated. The paper reports parameter counts and labels them as RAM usage, but does not measure peak training VRAM or total memory. Optimizer states, activations, replay buffers, normalization state, and framework overhead can materially change the claimed savings.

The most important missing baseline is a smaller target-based network matched to iS-QN's actual memory budget. Without this comparison, the experiments do not establish that sharing features is preferable to allocating the same constrained memory to a narrower conventional online/target pair.

The interpretation that the heads learn consecutive Bellman iterations is not theoretically justified under shared, continually changing features. A copied head does not represent a fixed prior Q-function when its feature extractor changes after every update, and no convergence or error analysis is provided.

K is a task-dependent hyperparameter, several values are evaluated, and the best-looking value varies substantially across settings. There is no held-out selection protocol, sensitivity analysis across tasks, or accounting for selection over multiple K values, weakening the headline comparisons.

Some comparisons are confounded by architecture or objective choices. Most notably, the continuous-control target-based baseline omits BatchNorm while target-free and iS variants use it; the K=9 loss is additionally discounted by a separately chosen factor. This makes it difficult to isolate the contribution of the proposed target-sharing mechanism.

The diagnostic evidence is correlational. Higher feature rank, lower target churn, and greater gradient similarity to the target-based method do not demonstrate that these quantities cause the performance gains; controlled interventions or stronger ablations are absent.

The claimed practical motivation concerns resource-constrained learning, yet experiments run on a high-end GPU and do not demonstrate that the method enables a larger model, batch, or task that a standard target-based method cannot fit. Thus, the practical significance of the memory savings remains uncertain.

Overall, the method and empirical breadth are promising, but the missing equal-memory baseline and lack of genuine memory measurements directly affect the paper's main claim. These issues place the work slightly below the acceptance threshold rather than supporting acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper introduces a simple, practically meaningful approach: retaining target copies only of small output heads while sharing the feature extractor substantially reduces Q-network parameter storage.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering online and offline RL, discrete and continuous control, Atari, DeepMind Control, and a language-based Wordle task. Across these settings, iS-QN consistently improves over the corresponding target-free baseline and often approaches or exceeds the target-based baseline.

The evaluation generally follows good deep-RL practice, including multiple seeds, IQM aggregation, stratified bootstrap confidence intervals, learning curves, per-task results, and parameter, runtime, and FLOP reporting.

The diagnostic analyses of gradient similarity, target churn, effective rank, and dormant neurons provide useful evidence about how shared target heads affect optimization and representation learning. The algorithm and hyperparameters are also described clearly, with code reportedly included in the supplement.
weaknesses: The resource-efficiency claim is supported mainly by parameter counts converted into nominal memory. Actual peak training memory is not measured, despite optimizer states, gradients, activations, replay buffers, normalization state, and framework overhead potentially changing the practical savings. Fixed-memory comparisons against a smaller target-based network are also missing.

Several controls needed to isolate the mechanism are absent. In particular, the paper does not compare against parameter-matched multi-head auxiliary objectives, heads trained toward the same target, partial target networks retaining multiple final layers, or a full iterated Q-Network baseline. Thus, the gains cannot be cleanly attributed to learning consecutive Bellman iterates rather than generic multi-head representation regularization.

The characterization of the heads as frozen targets is somewhat imprecise: although a head's parameters are frozen, its predictions change whenever the shared feature extractor changes. Consequently, the claim that the heads represent consecutive Bellman iterations is heuristic and is not backed by theoretical analysis or a direct measurement of Bellman-chain approximation quality.

Some evidence is narrower or confounded. Atari uses selected subsets of 10–15 games, Wordle is a single task with five seeds, and the continuous-control target-based baseline omits BatchNorm while the target-free and proposed methods use it. Moreover, normalized AUC uncertainty appears not to propagate uncertainty in the target-based denominator. These issues temper the otherwise convincing empirical case.

strengths: The paper introduces a simple and practically useful middle ground between target-free and target-network methods: retaining only frozen linear heads while sharing the feature extractor substantially reduces the parameter overhead of a full target network.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering online and offline Atari, continuous control, language-model-based offline RL, and streaming RL. Results generally show consistent improvements over the corresponding target-free baselines.

The main Atari experiments use multiple games, multiple seeds, IQM aggregation, stratified bootstrap confidence intervals, and per-game learning curves, providing substantially stronger evidence than a small collection of headline results.

The paper includes useful analyses of target churn, gradient alignment, representation rank, runtime, FLOPs, sensitivity to the number of heads, target-update period, mixed precision, and compatibility with MellowMax.

The presentation is clear, the method is easy to implement, and the appendix supplies detailed architectures, hyperparameters, environment protocols, and individual curves. Carbon impact and language-model use are also disclosed.
weaknesses: The experiments do not adequately isolate why multiple heads help. In discrete online RL, iS-DQN changes both the training objective and behavior policy by sampling actions from a randomly selected head. Controls with the same number of heads and losses but a common target, a fixed acting head, or parameter-matched auxiliary objectives are needed to distinguish iterated Bellman learning from ensemble-style exploration and generic multi-task representation learning. The success of the non-iterated ES-CQL variant further suggests that sharing and ensembling may explain part of the gain.

The central resource-efficiency claim is supported mainly by network parameter counts rather than measured peak training memory. Activations, optimizer state, replay storage, compilation buffers, and framework overhead can dominate actual RAM or VRAM, while the method retains essentially the same FLOPs and runtime. Peak-memory measurements and maximum feasible model or batch sizes would make the practical claim convincing.

Model selection is insufficiently controlled. Different settings use different selected values of K, and SAC additionally introduces a manually chosen 0.25 loss-discount factor. The paper does not describe a held-out tuning protocol or account for the cost of selecting these values, so comparisons involving the best variant may be optimistic.

Some comparisons are not architecture-matched. In particular, TF-SAC and iS-SAC use BatchNorm whereas TB-SAC does not, and normalization choices vary across the discrete experiments. Although the authors provide a motivation, this prevents a clean attribution of performance and memory differences solely to the proposed target construction.

The normalized-AUC definition is problematic for tasks with negative returns. Wordle uses rewards of -1 or 0 and reports negative performance throughout training, so dividing its raw AUC by the negative TB-ILQL AUC reverses the ordering: a better, less-negative AUC should produce a ratio below 100%, contrary to Figure 7. The manuscript must explain any unreported transformation or correct the metric and claims. More generally, uncertainty in the baseline denominator should be included by bootstrapping the normalized ratio jointly.

Claims that variants outperform target-based methods are sometimes stronger than the statistical evidence: several confidence intervals overlap substantially. The paper would benefit from paired comparisons or bootstrap intervals for the differences rather than relying on separately displayed intervals.

The method inherits an additional update period and introduces K, whose best value varies considerably across architectures and settings. Robustness of the target-update period is demonstrated on only one Atari game, while the recommendation to increase K until performance declines can require expensive environment-specific tuning.

Technical details for variants beyond hard-update DQN are scattered and incomplete. A unified algorithm specifying soft head updates, double critics or distributional heads, optimizer-state treatment when heads are copied, terminal masking, and the precise CQL, SAC, ILQL, and streaming objectives would improve reproducibility.

strengths: The core idea—retaining only target heads while sharing the feature extractor—is simple, intuitive, easy to implement, and practically relevant when critic parameters dominate memory.
The empirical study is unusually broad, spanning online and offline discrete control, continuous control, language-based RL, and streaming RL.
Results consistently show improvement over the corresponding target-free baselines, often recovering much of the gap to target-network methods.
The paper includes useful diagnostics on target churn, gradient similarity, representation rank, runtime, FLOPs, target-update frequency, feature width, and the number of heads.
Presentation is generally clear, and the appendix provides hyperparameters, per-task curves, confidence intervals, and a reproducibility statement.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited: the method largely combines partial target-network parameter sharing with the previously proposed iterated Q-network mechanism. There is no theoretical analysis establishing stability or convergence when nominally frozen heads operate on continually changing shared features.

The headline resource-efficiency claim is not adequately validated. The paper reports parameter-derived RAM estimates rather than measured peak accelerator memory, omitting optimizer states, activations, replay buffers, and framework overhead. Learned auxiliary heads also incur optimizer and activation storage, unlike a frozen target network. No experiment is performed on an actually memory-constrained device.

The number of Bellman iterations K is selected differently across settings after evaluating multiple candidates, without a held-out selection protocol or accounting for selection bias. The recommended procedure of increasing K until performance decreases weakens the claim of an immediately practical replacement and adds substantial tuning cost.

Comparisons are mostly limited to internally constructed target-based and target-free variants. Stronger comparisons against contemporary target-free methods, full iterated Q-learning, and memory- or compute-matched alternatives are missing. The MellowMax comparison covers only two games.

Several ablations are too narrow to establish robustness: target-update sensitivity is studied on one Atari game, width sensitivity on two games, meta-weighting on three games, and mixed precision on four games. The main Atari results also use selected subsets rather than the complete benchmark.

The Wordle evaluation appears internally inconsistent or at least seriously under-specified. Returns are negative under the stated reward definition, so directly dividing AUC by the target-based AUC does not preserve the claimed interpretation that values above 100% are better. This calls the reported improvement in that domain into question.

The mechanistic evidence is correlational. Higher effective rank, lower target churn, and greater gradient similarity do not establish that these quantities cause the performance gains, and pertinent controls such as auxiliary-head or representation-regularization baselines are absent.

Overall, the paper contains a promising practical heuristic and substantial experimentation, but limited novelty, post-hoc hyperparameter selection, insufficient memory measurement, and incomplete baselines leave the central claims short of the top-tier acceptance threshold.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering online and offline discrete control, continuous control, language-model-based offline RL, and streaming RL. Across these settings, iS-QN consistently improves upon target-free variants and often approaches or exceeds full target-network performance.

The Atari evaluation uses multiple games, multiple seeds, IQM aggregation, and stratified bootstrap confidence intervals. Per-game learning curves are supplied, reducing the risk that aggregate gains are driven by a small subset of tasks.

The paper includes useful ablations over the number of Bellman iterations, target-update period, representation width, loss weighting, normalization, mixed precision, and compatibility with MellowMax. The gradient-similarity, target-churn, and effective-rank analyses also provide plausible insight into why the method works.

The resource-performance tradeoff is compelling: the method often retains approximately target-free parameter counts while substantially recovering target-based performance. The Wordle and large-critic SAC experiments make this benefit particularly concrete.

The manuscript is clear and well organized, gives detailed hyperparameters and experimental protocols, promises code and dependencies in the supplementary material, and explicitly discusses limitations, runtime, FLOPs, carbon impact, and LLM usage.
weaknesses: The central resource-efficiency claim is supported primarily by parameter counts rather than measured peak training memory. Actual device memory also includes activations, optimizer state, replay buffers, framework overhead, and the additional heads; direct peak-memory measurements across representative workloads would make the practical claim substantially stronger.

The method introduces K as a setting-dependent hyperparameter, and the reported preferred values vary considerably across experiments. Because several K values are explored, some gains over the target-based baseline may partly reflect additional method-specific selection effort. A prespecified selection rule or validation-budget-controlled comparison would improve fairness.

The contribution is predominantly empirical and offers no convergence or stability analysis for the nonlinear shared-feature setting. Frozen heads are not truly fixed target functions because their shared representation changes after every update, so a more formal account of when this construction remains stable would strengthen the technical contribution.

Some evaluation components are narrow: Wordle is a single language task, the streaming study covers seven Atari games, and sensitivity to the target-update period is tested on only one game. These results establish promising breadth across domains but not yet strong generality within every domain.

The normalized AUC presentation is intuitive but can obscure absolute performance and statistical comparisons against the target-based baseline. Explicit paired differences or probability-of-improvement analyses, together with clearer uncertainty for the normalized ratios, would make claims such as outperforming the target-based approach more rigorous.

The method does not generally reduce training FLOPs or wall-clock time, and the manuscript acknowledges that it only reduces training-time network storage rather than inference memory. Thus, its practical advantage is specifically parameter-memory efficiency rather than broad computational efficiency.
